Jonathan Reynolds , the business secretary, has suggested the UK needs to know more about where the EU is heading before it signs up to a much closer relationship.
He made the comment in an interview with the Sun , a day after John Healey , the chancellor, also hinted that he might have reservations about Andy Burnham’s ambitions for a new relationship with the EU undoing the damage done by Brexit.
Burnham is attending a summit with the EU next month where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus. There is strong support for all these initiatives in cabinet.
But Burnham also wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election, when – if it wants – Labour will be able to dump the 2024 manifesto pledges ruling out joining the single market or the customs union.
Burnham has not said what he wants to propose in Labour’s next manifesto, and he insists ultimately the public will decide, but he has said that he would like the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime and he seems open to trying to rejoin the single market in the next parliament.
Asked by the Sun if he shared Burnham’s dream of rejoining the EU, Reynolds replied:
double quotation mark I genuinely can’t answer that, because I don’t know what the future of the EU is – because [of] some of the very strong political currents in member states.
For me, it’s an approach to issues. What is their approach to how they regulate technology, AI ? How dynamic will the economy be?
Sophia Sleigh , who wrote up the comments, said Reynolds was referring to the rise of far-right populist parties in Europe, which could fundamentally change and weaken the EU.
Although Reynolds’ comments were prompted by a question about rejoining the EU, his concerns would also apply to a proposal to join the single market.
Healey is also distinctly less pro-European than Burnham. In interviews yesterday, he did not accept that joining the single market would automatically be good for growth , he stressed the importance of accepting the referendum decision and making the best of the current relationship, and said he did not expect the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime .
In a bid to stop ministers disagreeing in public about the EU, Burnham sent them a letter earlier this week telling them to stay “disciplined” and not to “advocate for specific options” as the debate on the future UK-EU relationship gets under way.

John Swinney , Scotland’s first minister, has now issued a statement about today’s national economic council [NEC] in Glasgow, and Downing Street has issued a readout about Andy Burnham ’s bilateral meeting with Swinney. Reading them together, three points emerge.
Swinney and Burnham were both positive about the meeting, and sounded keen to be constructive not confrontational. No 10 said both leaders agreed the NEC meeting had been “extremely positive”, and Swinney said it was “a welcome start of work to develop the UK government’s new principle of ‘devolving by default’”.

For the record, here is the full readout from the No 10 spokesperson .
double quotation mark The prime minister met with the first minister of Scotland in Glasgow following a meeting of the National Economic Council today.
The prime minister and first minister agreed the meeting at the NEC had been extremely positive. They said it had been a valuable exercise in starting the process of exploring how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode.
They agreed that now there would be a policy sprint led by No 10 North, involving officials from both governments, to take this agenda forward.
Outside that process, the prime minister said the UK government would review and respond to a range of issues raised by the first minister.
This would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland, which the prime minister has repeatedly made clear is off the table.
double quotation mark While the prime minister and I disagree on independence, we do agree that Westminster does not work for people in Scotland. And when the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will come about.
To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with him to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland – as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living.
Today’s meeting of the national economic council was a welcome start of work to develop the UK Government’s new principle of ‘devolving by default’ and the prime minister has been clear that he will not bypass the Scottish parliament in this endeavour.
I welcome that commitment, and look forward to our governments jointly developing a plan to consider further devolution to Scotland that will boost economic growth.
A rise in rough sleeping in London is a “stark reminder of the huge challenge” Andy Burnham faces in his pledge to get people off the streets, campaigners have said. As the Press Association reports, data shows there were 4,678 people recorded as sleeping rough in the capital in July to September this year. PA says:
double quotation mark While this is a slight drop of 1% on the same three-month period in 2025, the figure has risen by almost a fifth (18%) on the previous quarter this year.
The Combined Homelessness and Information Network (Chain) figures, published today , showed that there were 819 people classed as living on the streets (a separate category) – a rise of 8% on the same time last year and up by a fifth (20%) on the previous quarter.
Rick Henderson, chief executive of Homeless Link , the national membership body for frontline homelessness services, said: “The increase in rough sleeping across London, and particularly of those spending longer on our streets, is a stark reminder of the huge challenge London and the wider country face in turning the prime minister’s ambition to end rough sleeping into action.”
Speaking to reporters after the national economic council meeting, Andy Burnham said he did not want Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to lose out on the changes that will give more financial powers to mayors in England.
Referring to the plans in the fiscal devolution roadmap , he said:
double quotation mark The agenda is moving quickly in England. There were further measures in the budget around regional devolution across all of England, and I don’t want to see Scotland left behind. I don’t want to see Wales left behind, but also crucially, I don’t want to see Northern Ireland left behind.
So it’s really important that we all move at the same pace together. And I won’t allow anything to delay that. Growth can’t wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK.
Referring to the absence of Northern Ireland’s first minister and deputy first minister, he said:
double quotation mark It’s disappointing that the first minister and deputy first minister of Northern Ireland weren’t here. There was some representation, but we will continue the discussions too with Stormont about how do we take forward the same ideas.
Andy Burnham has said the UK government will consider further devolution of employment support to Scotland and Wales.
Speaking after chairing a meeting of the national economic council, Burnham said:
double quotation mark We had a good discussion today on two fronts.
One around reindustrialisation, and the offer of more devolution of innovation funding to the regional level. It’s about creating those structures at a regional level, and that’s a matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries.
It’s not for me to impose or try to interfere there. But once there is a vehicle, that can be backed by the Scottish government, it can be backed by the UK government …
Secondly, we had a conversation about employment support, and particularly young people. There are too many young people out of work here in Scotland, in Wales, and in England too.
It’s a very big agenda that’s coming towards us. We need to localise as much as we can support for young people, employment support to help them back to work.
Now, as part of those discussions that will follow this meeting of the national economic council, we need to look at what are [the] arrangements for further devolution of employment support, particularly for young people in both Scotland and Wales.

At the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson was asked to give more details of the sort of “regional empowerment” that could be offered to Scotland and Wales on the basis of today’s summit. The spokesperson did not give any detail beyond what No 10 has said already (see 9.11am ) and, like the PM (see 12.05pm ), he said it was ultimately up to Scotland and Wales to say what they wanted. It sounds like we won’t be getting specific proposals today.
Downing Street has paid tribute to Patrick Stewart following the actor’s death. At the daily lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson gave a comment that was a bit more extensive than the usual No 10 contribution when a great British celebrity dies. The spokesperson said that was because Andy Burnham feels strongly about the importance of actors.
double quotation mark The prime minister was very sad to hear of the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart.
As a former culture secretary he knows how much Britain’s greatest actors mean to the country, and Sir Patrick was one of the very best.
He never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots. He brought joy to millions, and he always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.
Our thoughts are with his family and friends.

Lee Waters , a former Labour minister in the Welsh government and a member of the Senedd until May this year, thinks it is a mistake for Andy Burnham to think Manchester-style devolution (greater powers for mayors) will help in Wales. Referring to posts earlier summarising Burnham’s thinking (see 9.11am , 9.33am and 12.05pm ), Waters sent me this note.
double quotation mark Just a reminder that when it comes to Wales, we are not comparing like with like. The term ‘region’ in an English context typically refers to an area covering between 1.5 and 3 million people. In Wales, regions cover much less dense areas. The Swansea Bay city region captures some 700,000 people, and similarly North Wales around 690,000 people. In Mid-Wales sheep outnumber people by 7:1. Only the Cardiff city region is comparable to English tiers, and even then at the lower end: around 1.5 million people.
Transposing an English mayoral worldview onto a very different political geography just doesn’t work. Wales may be a similar population size to the PM’s old manor but that’s where the parallel ends. Andy Burnham talks about the regions of England and Wales interchangeably but the role the new prime minister champions for metro mayors is, in many respects, already performed by the Welsh government. Powers over skills, employment support, economic development, housing investment and major spending programmes sit at an all-Wales strategic level (covering a similar population size to Greater Manchester.)
